Cover and
of seeded wheatgrass species is much improved in 2014 over what was present at the end of the
2013 growing season. Little change in cover of seeded wheatgrass species was observed in
2015, however frequency was slightly higher. Cheatgrass cover was low but frequency was
much higher in 2015. Canby bluegrass was not detected in the transects. Little evidence of
grazing was present.

another 5%. Annual and undesirable forbs averaged 5%. Though the cover of cheatgrass was

that seeded poa species rarely establish, although in this case the amount of poa in the seed mix
was very low. Also, seeding rates of 11 to 15 lbs. per acre pure live seed seem to work best for
obtaining cover values of 20% or higher for a primarily wheatgrass seed mix. Other sagebrush
and greasewood dominated areas not seeded have recovered fairly well with native grasses and
greasewood is re-establishing itself in the alkaline drainage bottoms.

A “standard “mix was designed to provide

Objectives:
To establish native perennial vegetation within the burn perimeter in order to limit the amount of nonnative
invasive species cover post burn. The treatment objective would be met when seeded Perennial species
achieve 10-15% canopy cover of seeded species after the first growing season. Within three years the monitoring
objective will be to achieve 80% canopy cover of native desirable species compared to the adjacent unburned
ecological sites.
Planned_Implementation:
Approximately 5,094 acres of the 9,963 acres burned on BLM lands will be aerially seeded with
either a fixed wing or rotor wing aircraft. Approximately 1,146 acres will be seeded with two
kinds of seed mix: more diverse seed mix designed to be more beneficial for wildlife and a
standard mix designed to both benefit wildlife and livestock as well as stabilize soils. The
seeding effort is expected to take between 5 and 15 days depending on the number of aircraft the
contractor utilizes on the project. The 6,400 acres identified for seeding represent the most
ecologically productive sandy loam soils that were formerly closed canopy pinion juniper. These
areas are also some of the deepest soils with the greatest potential for soil loss due to erosion.
The proposed seed mixes and rate is listed in Table 1 and the areas identified for seeding are
shown on Map 2.
Actual_Implementation:
Colorado Parks and Wildlife provided $280,000 worth of seed
purchase which procured approximately 66% of the seed put on the
ground.
Mule Deer foundation procured 3,200 lbs of 4-wing saltbush 5% of
the seed put on the ground.
BLM procured 19,300 lbs of seed (29%), contracted the mixing,
transportation, and aerial application.

Using existing vegetation maps, NRCS soil survey data, burn severity map, proposed seeding
polygons were delineated specifically targeting ecological sites that are known to have lower
resistance to invasive species invasion following fire, and are less resilient to disturbances such
as fire, drought, and insects (Map 2). This information was also used in conjunction with
Ecological Site Descriptions (ESD), to determine appropriate seed mixes. Seeded species are
based on site potential, approximate plant functional/structural group distribution for the early
seral state and transition model of the ESDs, while considering seed availability and cost.
Dominant grass species were selected based on site potential and ESDs. Forbs selected are based
on the site as well as what CPW desired to have established to meet their desired objectives.
Two seed mixes were derived by BLM and CPW. A “standard “mix was designed to provide
baseline approximation of important early seral grasses, forbs, and shrubs found within the burn
area. The standard seed mix area totaled 3,948 acres (40% of BLM lands burned). Sites were
selected based on soil productivity and accessibility for livestock and wildlife. A second
“wildlife” seed mix was developed by CPW that included 9 additional forbs, one additional
grass, and antelope bitter brush and mountain mahogany which was designed to achieve desired
wildlife habitat objectives. The wildlife seed mix area totaled 1,146 acres (11% of the burn area
on BLM). Sites were selected based on soil productivity and areas that were less accessible by
domestic livestock. 49% of the burn area was not seeded, these areas were steep slopes,
productive resprouting mixed mountain shrub communities, or aspen/Douglas fir communities
that are inherently more resistant to invasive species dominance and more resilient to
disturbances such as fire.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2/25/19: After one growing season the Standard seed mix strata appears to be
nearing maximum percent bare ground for the ESDs with an average bare ground value of 32%
(Figure 5). Oddly, the wildlife seed mix strata (59%) has greater bare ground than the unseeded
strata (49%). Bare ground values in the standard seed mix strata ranged between 19%-49%,
unseeded values ranged between 40%-55%, and the wildlife seed mix strata had bare round
values between 50%-65% (figure 6). The differences between the standard and wildlife mix
strata are odd given that both mixes had the same base seed mix. With the additional species that
were added to the wildlife mix, this should have helped to achieve less bare ground than the
unseeded areas. It will be interesting to see moving forward if this trend reverses. With continued
progress it appears that all three strata will achieve 80% of the ESD reference of 36% bare
ground within three growing seasons.

The Bull Draw ES&R plan set an objective of achieving 10-15% canopy cover of seeded/native
species cover within the first growing season. Figure 7 shows that both seeded strata far
exceeded this objective. With the exceptionally wet and cool spring the unseeded strata also
exceeded this objective. While all three strata exceeded the desired objective the two seeded
strata had nearly 30% greater seeded native species cover than did the unseeded strata suggesting
that seeding was a net benefit for stabilizing soils and developing a competitive plant community
capable of resisting invasion by non-native species. Unlike bare ground there was no clear
difference in native species cover between the standard and wildlife mix strata with average
cover values of 18.0 and 19.2. Of the 13 monitoring plots established in the Bull Draw fire only
one Standard seed mix plot failed to meet the 1st year objective of obtaining 10-15% canopy
cover of desirable native species (Figure 8). While all three strata met the 1st year objective
figure 8 shows that on average seeded sites had far greater native species cover than did the
unseeded sites.

Figures 9 and 10 show the percent cover of forbs and grasses. In the case of both functional
groups the cover values far exceed the unseeded sites and adjacent unburned sites. These two
functional groups play a key role in resisting invasion by cheatgrass and alyssum and appear to
be on a good trajectory of achieving desired outcomes from the decision to seed the burn areas.
All strata had more native perennial forb cover than the unburned controls. The standard and
wildlife seed mix areas had greater grass cover than the unburned controls as well and
significantly greater grass cover than the unseeded strata. The mean cover of invasive non-native
plants remained low through the 1st growing season with only the standard mix strata having a
mean cover greater than 6% (figure 11). The unseeded and wildlife mix strata have mean
invasive species cover values below 2% and comparable to the unburned controls sites.

The seeding achieved a mean of 0.12 forbs per meter squared for the standard seed mix and 0.25
forbs/m2 for the wildlife seed mix (Figure 12). Suggesting that adding the additional more
expensive forbs to the wildlife mix has resulted in nearly double the number of forbs present on
the ground. None of the native forbs seeded were observed in the unseeded plots.
The seeding achieved a mean of 6 grasses/m2 in the standard mix and 4.7 grasses/m2 in the
wildlife mix (figure 13) which is more than adequate to resist invasion from cheatgrass assuming
these densities persist, the unseeded areas had a mean of 1.5 grasses/ m2. The mean density of
seeded shrubs in the standard mix was 0.13 plants/m2 and for the wildlife mix 0.45 plant/m2
(Figure 14). The mean of 0.45 was artificially driven up by one plot recording a shrub density of
2.3 plants/m2 with the other four plots having shrub densities below 0.12 plant/m2. None of the
seeded shrubs from either mix were observed in the unseeded strata.

With greater percent cover values of grasses, forbs, and shrubs than unseeded areas and with
greater plant densities than unseeded areas after the 1st growing season it appears that seeding
was justified given the costs. With greater cover values and plant densities in seeded areas than
unseeded sites these areas are on a trajectory to have a greater ability to resist invasive species
and meet more quickly meet CPW desired objectives of better winter range forage for mule deer.

ESR 2022 Monitoring Report
MONITORING RESULTS
Benchmark objectives were derived from the ecological site R048AY405UT Mountain Loam,
which encompassed one plot. Ecological site descriptions data for R048AY342UT Upland Very
Steep Shallow Loam, which encompass the other two plots, was not available at the time of
writing this report.
Seed Mix Species Demographics:
Approximately half of the seeded species were present at the sites (Figure 17), with the majority
of them showing up as seedlings (1.3 \xb1 0.03 individuals/m2 seedlings; 0.2 \xb1 0.007
individuals/m2 established). The species with the greatest mean density in 2021 was Elymus
trachycaulus (ELTR7; estimated average: 0.8 \xb1 0.02 individuals/m2), followed by Elymus
elymoides (ELEL5; estimated average: 0.3 \xb1 0.08 individuals/m2), and Balsamorhiza sagittata
(BASA3; estimated average: 0.2 \xb1 0.03 individuals/m2). When accounting for uncertainty at the
seedling stage it is unclear which species occurred at the greatest density (Figure 17).

Seed Mix Functional Group Demographics:
Grasses were clearly at a higher total density than both forbs and shrubs, and forbs were found at
a greater total density than shrubs (Figure 18). Seeded grasses (estimated average: 1.2 \xb1 0.02
individuals/m2) were more abundant than seeded forbs (estimated average: 0.3 \xb1 0.01
individuals/m2) and shrubs (estimated average: 0.0 individuals/m2). Seedlings were found at a
higher density than established plants. Although, there was considerable uncertainty around
some estimates which makes it unclear if there was a difference between seedlings and
established plants, specifically (Figure 18).

Perennial grasses relevant to rangeland readiness were found to occur at an estimated average
total density of 0.6 \xb1 0.02 individuals/m2 (Figure 20). All of which consists of individuals
without seed heads from three species: Elymus elmoides (ELEL5; estimated average: 0.3 \xb1 0.08
individuals/m2), Sporobolus cryptantha (SPCR; estimated average: 0.2 \xb1 0.1 individuals/m2), and
Achnatherum nelsonii (ACHY; estimated average: 0.04 \xb1 0.01 individuals/m2) (Figure 19).

Seed Mix Species Demographics:
Seeded species demographic responses varied, with most seeded species absent, and no clear
differences between species (Figure 28). The species with the greatest mean density in 2021 was
Poa secunda (POSE; estimated average: 4.7 \xb1 1.2 individuals/m2), followed by Oenothera
pallida (OEPA; estimated average: 2.2 \xb1 0.6 individuals/m2), Elymus trachycaulus (ELTR7;
estimated average: 1.0 \xb1 0.2 individuals/m2), and Elymus lanceolatus (ELLA3; estimated
average: 0.2 \xb1 0.05 individuals/m2). Again, when accounting for uncertainty it is unclear which
species occurred at the greatest density (Figure 28).

Seed Mix Functional Group Demographics:
There was considerable uncertainty around estimates, making it unclear if there was a difference
between seedlings and established plants, as well as whether there was a difference between
functional groups (Figure 29).
Seeded grasses (estimated average: 5.9 \xb1 0.6 individuals/m2) were more abundant than seeded
forbs (estimated average: 2.3 \xb1 0.2 individuals/m2) and shrubs (estimated average: 0.0 \xb1 0.0
individuals/m2), and seedlings were generally found at a higher density than established plants
